name: Reaching Families Who Are Hardest to Reach
title: Reaching Families Who Are Hardest to Reach
answer: Schools often fail to reach the families who need them most, because the parents with the greatest needs are the least likely to actually receive school messages. This idea asks schools to track who is genuinely receiving and opening messages, to keep contact details current, and to let families choose how they are contacted. It matters because a message that never arrives cannot help anyone, and trust with wary families is built slowly through honest, consistent contact.

sections.body: The idea starts from a hard truth: the families schools most need to reach are frequently the hardest to reach. A trial using existing messaging platforms found that the neediest parents were the least likely to receive messages, because phone numbers change, email addresses go unchecked, and some families simply do not use the apps schools prefer. The problem this solves is the false comfort of sending a message and assuming it landed. Instead of treating delivery as success, schools check who is actually receiving and reading, and they treat contact as something to be maintained rather than assumed. The aim is to close the gap between the families a school intends to reach and the families it actually reaches.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, schools look at the delivery and read reports most messaging platforms already produce, and they break those reports out by school and by language so gaps become visible. Families who never open messages are then followed up in other ways, such as a phone call, a home visit, or a note sent home with the child. AI can help identify which families need that outreach, but the contact itself is made by people. Contact information is refreshed regularly rather than only at enrollment, with a short reminder each semester asking families to confirm their phone number and preferred language. Families are also allowed to choose how they want to be reached, on the principle that meeting families where they are works better than expecting them to use the school's preferred channel. The text does not give separate grade band guidance for this idea.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with a trial finding rather than a broad research base. It states that the trial using existing messaging platforms found that the neediest parents were the least likely to receive messages, attributed to Musaddiq et al., 2023. The text offers no other study, figure, or statistic for this idea, so the rest of the guidance rests on practice and on the reported delivery and read rates that messaging platforms themselves provide.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets out clear limits. Some families distrust messages from institutions, sometimes for good reason, and immigrant families may worry about how their information is used, especially in times of heightened immigration enforcement. Schools should therefore explain plainly what information they collect and why. Trust is described as something that grows slowly, through communication that is consistent, honest, and respectful. The decisions about who to contact and how to make that contact stay with people, while AI is limited to helping identify which families to reach out to.
